review: Chandratal at dawn with nobody else around was worth every hour on that road. The homestay in Kibber fed us better than most restaurants.
Tenzin paced the first days well and nobody in our group had altitude trouble. Tabo monastery was the surprise of the trip.
Stunning, but be honest with yourself about the road days. Eight hours in a jeep over Kunzum is hard on the back.
I liked that our money visibly went to the villages. We were shown the fodder bank and met the people who run it.
Cold nights even in July and the dry toilets take a day to get used to. The night sky made up for both.
Went in the second week of August and the valley was pink and blue from end to end. Our botanist could name everything.
It rained on four days out of six, exactly as the description warned. Good rain gear matters more than good boots here.
The climb to Hemkund is brutal and optional and I am glad I did it. Porters were paid fairly and treated as part of the group.
Ghangaria is basic and crowded with pilgrims. The valley itself is quiet once you walk past the first kilometre.
A small group made all the difference on a narrow trail. We saw a brahma kamal on the last day.
Eleven rhinos before breakfast on the first morning. Rohan spotted a fishing cat that I would have driven straight past.
I appreciated that there was no elephant riding. The lodge naturalists were former forest guards with thirty years of stories.
The western range was the best for wildlife, the eastern for birds. The drive from Guwahati is longer than I expected.
Hearing the gibbons call at Hoollongapar was the highlight for my kids. Easy trip to do with a family.
Dusty in February, so carry a scarf. Wildlife sightings were constant and the jeeps were never crowded.
No tiger, and it did not matter. Drifting through the creeks at high tide in silence is something I will remember.
The boat is simple and the cabins are small. Food cooked on board was excellent, especially the fish.
The evening with the mangrove cooperative changed how I think about this place. We planted our saplings ourselves.
Great for birds. Six kingfisher species as promised, plus a crocodile on the mudbank at Dobanki.
Peaceful, but three days of watchtowers was one too many for me. Would suit people who like slow travel.
The stairs to Nongriat are no joke and my legs shook for two days. Sleeping in the village after the day trippers leave is magic.
Banri's family has looked after one of the bridges for generations and he explained how the roots are trained. Unforgettable.
Very humid and the trail is slippery. The natural pools near the double-decker bridge were the reward.
Dawki's water really is that clear. I liked that village fees were paid in front of us, straight to the council.
Well organised and well paced. Mawlynnong felt a little staged compared with Nongriat.
Walking out on the salt under a full moon is surreal. The bhungas stay warm at night even when it is freezing outside.
Loved buying directly from the weavers. The Rann itself is busier than the photos suggest, but our guide knew a quiet stretch.
Thousands of flamingos and common cranes at Chhari Dhand. Imran is a patient guide and a very good birder.
An easy, comfortable trip. More driving than walking, which suited my parents.
The village-run resort was the right choice over the big tent city. Food was simple Kutchi home cooking.
The walk in Periyar with former poachers was the most interesting day I have had on any trip. They read the forest like a book.
Saw Nilgiri tahr within minutes at Eravikulam and a herd of elephants from the bamboo raft. Lakshmi was superb.
Leeches. So many leeches in September. The leech socks work, wear them.
The long day through the shola forest was tougher than moderate in my opinion. Beautiful all the same.
Misty mornings, tea estates and good filter coffee. A well-thought-out route with very little time in a vehicle.
Doing the morning reef counts made me look far more closely than I would have alone. I can now tell a parrotfish from a wrasse.
Kayaking through the mangroves with the water glowing under the paddle was unreal. Small group, no crowds.
Reefs at Shaheed Dweep were healthier than at Swaraj Dweep. Ferry timings ate into one day.
Strict about not touching coral and not feeding fish, which I respect. Saw a turtle on three separate snorkels.
Lovely, though pricey once you add flights. The biologist travelling with us was worth it.
On day seven a female and two cubs crossed the ridge opposite our camp. Three hours through the scope. I cried.
We did not see a leopard and I would still recommend it. Wolves, ibex, and a family in Rumbak who treated us like relatives.
The trackers are extraordinary. They found a cat asleep on a ledge that I could not see even when told where to look.
The coldest I have ever been and the best wildlife trip I have ever taken. Take the acclimatisation days seriously.
Minus eighteen at night in a homestay with one stove. Bring a proper sleeping bag liner. Sightings on two days.
Walking in tiger country sharpens every sense. We found fresh pugmarks over our own footprints on the way back.
The canoe at sunset on the Denwa, with skimmers flying past, was perfect. Hardly another vehicle all week.
The mobile camp is properly basic, one bucket of water and no power. That is the point, but know before you go.
Sloth bear with a cub on her back from about eighty metres, on foot. The forest guard kept us calm and safe.
A thoughtful alternative to the busy parks. The rock paintings near Pachmarhi were an unexpected bonus.
